headline_marked: [[Desktop GPU shipments hit 4-year high]] of 12.5M units in Q2 2026; Nvidia secures 90% market share
headline: Desktop GPU shipments hit 4-year high of 12.5M units in Q2 2026; Nvidia secures 90% market share
summary: Despite rising prices and a drop in CPU sales, discrete graphics card sales surged, driven by gamers anticipating further price increases. Nvidia dominates with a 90% market share.
details: Discrete graphics card shipments for desktop PCs reached 12.5 million units in Q2 2026, marking the highest number since Q1 2022. This surge occurred despite record-high prices and declining desktop CPU shipments, according to Jon Peddie Research.

The industry saw a 5.9% sequential and 7.8% year-over-year increase in shipments. The first half of 2026 shipped 24.3 million desktop AIBs, significantly up from 20.8 million in the first half of 2025, indicating a stronger year for unit sales despite price hikes.

Analysts note that only about 14 million desktop PCs were sold during the quarter, with an unusually high 89% attach rate. This suggests that the majority of AIBs were purchased by gamers in retail, rather than for new PC builds, as consumers rushed to buy before prices increased further due to global events.

Nvidia maintained its dominant position, shipping approximately 11.25 million discrete GPUs for desktop computers in Q2 2026, securing about 90% market share. AMD held roughly 8% with one million units, while Intel's share rose to 2% with several hundred thousand units.

This quarter was particularly strong for Nvidia, marking its highest quantity of discrete desktop GPU sales since Q3 2017. In contrast, AMD's standalone graphics card sales have generally remained around one million units per quarter for nearly four years, though Q2 2026 showed an improvement over Q2 2025.

Overall, Nvidia shipped approximately 17.365 million discrete graphics processors in Q2 2026, including 11.25 million for desktops and 6.115 million for notebooks and compact PCs. Both AMD and Intel have largely exited the market for standalone mobile GPUs.

headline_marked: [[I fixed a John Deere tractor]] using their self-repair service, but farmers aren't sold on it
headline: I fixed a John Deere tractor using their self-repair service, but farmers aren't sold on it
summary: John Deere's Pro Service, introduced in 2025, allows owners to diagnose and fix complex machinery. However, annual fees starting at $195 and a history of repair restrictions leave many farmers skeptical.
details: The author successfully fixed a water-in-fuel sensor on a John Deere tractor in minutes using the company's new Operations Center Pro Service software. This hands-on experience demonstrated the service's capability for simple repairs.

John Deere's CTO, Jahmy Hindman, presented the Pro Service as "owner-friendly," aiming to address long-standing right-to-repair criticisms. The service pairs with nearly all electronic-enabled John Deere machines.

For years, John Deere has been a primary target of the right-to-repair movement due to digital locks on its high-tech agricultural machinery. These restrictions often required official dealer approval for even basic repairs or aftermarket part installation.

The company recently faced multiple lawsuits, including a $99 million settlement for burdensome repair costs and an FTC settlement requiring improved repairability. Critics argue these measures are insufficient to truly change Deere's practices.

Pro Service, introduced in 2025, starts at an annual cost of $195 per machine, or up to $5,995 for full fleet access for larger operations. It allows owners to connect software via Wi-Fi or cable to diagnose issues using manuals and data services.

John Deere also plans to integrate an AI chatbot called JD into the Operations Center to further assist users in finding repair information. Modern tractors can have upwards of 50 controllers, making diagnostics increasingly complex.

Despite these efforts, many farmers remain unconvinced, citing the high subscription costs and the company's past resistance. The core issue of full, unrestricted access to repair tools and information persists for many advocates.
